deck.title: The Trial Balance & Correction of Errors

front_blocks.md: Define a **trial balance**.

back_blocks.md: A **trial balance** is a statement listing **all the accounts and their balances** on a particular date, each in either a debit or a credit column. The two column totals should be **equal**.

cards.front_md: Define a **trial balance**.
cards.back_md: A **trial balance** is a statement listing **all the accounts and their balances** on a particular date, each in either a debit or a credit column. The two column totals should be **equal**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The trial balance is part of the double entry system.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
It is a **statement** drawn up from the ledger balances, not a ledger account. Nothing is ever posted to it, which is why it can be redrafted without affecting the accounts themselves.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

The trial balance is part of the double entry system.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

It is a **statement** drawn up from the ledger balances, not a ledger account. Nothing is ever posted to it, which is why it can be redrafted without affecting the accounts themselves.

front_blocks.md: Give two uses of a trial balance.

back_blocks.md: A trial balance:

- checks for **arithmetic errors** in the ledger accounts, since a miscalculated balance will usually stop the totals agreeing
- gathers every balance **in one place**, which helps with preparing the financial statements

front_blocks.md: Which balance in a trial balance is always the opening figure, and why?

back_blocks.md: The **inventory** balance is always the opening figure. The current inventory sits inside the **purchases** account until the year-end transfer, so the inventory account still shows last year's closing value.

front_blocks.md: Name three accounts that appear in the debit column of a trial balance.

back_blocks.md: Debit balances include:

- **purchases** and **sales returns**
- expenses such as rent paid, discount allowed and carriage
- **trade receivables**, the **bank**, and other assets including inventory
- **drawings**

front_blocks.md: Name three accounts that appear in the credit column of a trial balance.

back_blocks.md: Credit balances include:

- **sales** and **purchases returns**
- other income such as rent received and discount received
- **trade payables**, a **bank overdraft**, and other liabilities such as a bank loan
- **capital**

front_blocks.md: A trial balance lists inventory of \$7060, but that is the year-end figure and the opening figure was \$2000 lower. What should it show?

back_blocks.md: The trial balance should show **\$5060**. It always carries the **opening** inventory, so \$7060 − \$2000 = **\$5060**.

front_blocks.md: Name the six types of error that do not affect the trial balance.

back_blocks.md: The six are:

- error of **omission**
- error of **original entry**
- error of **complete reversal**
- error of **commission**
- error of **principle**
- **compensating** errors

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A trial balance that agrees proves the ledger accounts are free of errors.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Six kinds of error leave the trial balance **still agreeing**, because the debit and credit totals are unaffected. Agreement shows only that the two totals match, not that every entry is right.

front_blocks.md: Why can an error that does not affect the trial balance still not be ignored?

back_blocks.md: It can misstate the **profit**, the **value of assets and liabilities**, or the balances owed to and from **other businesses**. An error that hides from the trial balance is still an error in the accounts.

front_blocks.md: Define a **posting error**.

back_blocks.md: A **posting error** is where **both entries** for a transaction are made on the **same side**, either both debits or both credits. Paying rent and debiting both the rent account and the bank account is an example.

front_blocks.md: Name the four kinds of error that do affect the trial balance.

back_blocks.md: They are:

- **addition** errors
- **posting** errors
- **unequal posting** errors
- **partial omission** errors

front_blocks.md: Define an **unequal posting error**.

back_blocks.md: An **unequal posting error** is where a transaction is entered into the two accounts using **different amounts**. Only one of the two figures can be right, so the trial balance will not agree.

front_blocks.md: Define an **addition error**.

back_blocks.md: An **addition error** is a **numerical mistake** made when balancing an account, or when totalling the debit or credit column of the trial balance. Totalling \$550 and \$450 as \$910 is an example.

front_blocks.md: Define a **partial omission error**.

back_blocks.md: A **partial omission error** is where a transaction is entered **only once**, so either the debit or the credit is missing. Debiting drawings for goods taken but forgetting to credit purchases is an example.

back_blocks.md: The unrecorded rent is an error of **omission**. The office expenses debited to an asset account instead of an expense account is an error of **principle**.

front_blocks.md: What two things must you establish before correcting any error?

back_blocks.md: How the accounts **currently look** with the error in them, and how they **should look** if the transaction had been entered correctly. The correcting entry is whatever turns the first into the second.

front_blocks.md: What must the narrative say on a journal entry that corrects an error?

back_blocks.md: It states **Correction of error**, followed by a brief description of what actually went wrong. That is what lets someone reading the accounts later understand why the entry is there.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A journal entry correcting an error must still have equal debits and credits.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
A correction is a journal entry like any other, so the debit total must equal the credit total. If it does not, the correction has introduced an error of its own.

front_blocks.md: Define a **suspense account**.

back_blocks.md: A **suspense account** is a **temporary** account opened when the trial balance totals do **not** agree. It holds the difference until the errors that caused it have been found and corrected.

front_blocks.md: Which side of the suspense account does the difference go on?

back_blocks.md: The side matching the **lower total** on the trial balance, labelled **Difference on trial balance**. That is what makes the suspense account's own two sides equal to begin with.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Every error is corrected through the suspense account.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Only errors that made the trial balance **disagree** go through it. The six errors that leave the totals agreeing are corrected without the suspense account being touched at all.

front_blocks.md: What does it mean if the suspense account will not balance after all the known errors are corrected?

back_blocks.md: There are still **unidentified errors** somewhere in the accounts. A suspense account that closes to zero is the signal that every error affecting the trial balance has been found.

front_blocks.md: How can you find the original difference on a trial balance when you are not given the trial balance itself?

back_blocks.md: Correct all the errors through the suspense account, then **balance** it. The balancing figure is the original difference, and the side it falls on is the side that was **smaller**.

back_blocks.md: **Credit** the supplier a further **\$270**, the difference between \$850 and \$580. **Debit** the suspense account \$270, because the original error left the credit total too low.

front_blocks.md: Define an **error of omission**.

back_blocks.md: An **error of omission** is where a transaction is **not entered into any ledger account** at all. The transaction is simply missing from the records.

front_blocks.md: Why does an error of omission leave the trial balance still agreeing?

back_blocks.md: The transaction is missing from the debit total and from the credit total **alike**. Since neither side has it, the two totals still match.

front_blocks.md: How do you correct an error of omission?

back_blocks.md: Simply enter the transaction **correctly**, exactly as it should have been recorded in the first place. Nothing has to be undone, because nothing was ever entered.

front_blocks.md: Define an **error of original entry**.

back_blocks.md: An **error of original entry** is where a transaction is entered into **both** ledger accounts using the **same wrong amount**. The accounts and the sides are right; only the figure is wrong.

back_blocks.md: The **same wrong figure** has gone into the debit total and the credit total. Both sides are wrong by the same amount, so they still match each other.

back_blocks.md: Find the **difference** between the wrong amount and the right one, and enter that difference in both accounts. Put it on the **same side** as the original entry to increase the figure, or on the **opposite side** to decrease it.

front_blocks.md: Define an **error of complete reversal**.

back_blocks.md: An **error of complete reversal** is where a transaction is entered on the **wrong sides** of the ledger accounts. The account that should have been debited was credited, and the one that should have been credited was debited.

front_blocks.md: Why does an error of complete reversal leave the trial balance still agreeing?

back_blocks.md: There is still **one debit and one credit** of the right amount. They are simply on the wrong sides, which the trial balance cannot detect.

front_blocks.md: Define an **error of commission**.

back_blocks.md: An **error of commission** is where one entry goes into the **wrong account**, but into an account of the **right type**. A credit sale posted to the wrong customer's account is the standard example.

back_blocks.md: **Undo** the entry in the wrong account by making an equal entry on the **opposite side**. Then make the entry in the **correct** account.

front_blocks.md: Define **compensating errors**.
